notes: `showmount -e <ip>` lists exports. Mount with `mount -t nfs <ip>:/share ./mnt -o nolock`. no_root_squash exports are a privesc goldmine (create a SUID root binary). UIDs map by number - match the owner UID locally to read files.
name: NFS - Enumeration & Mounting
description: List NFS exports, scan the RPC/NFS ports, then mount the share and inspect ownership. ls -n shows raw UID/GID (useful when the export trusts UIDs, e.g. no_root_squash).

steps.label: 1. Show exports + scan
steps.command:
showmount -e 10.129.14.128
sudo nmap 10.129.14.128 -p111,2049 -sV -sC
sudo nmap --script nfs* 10.129.14.128 -sV -p111,2049

steps.label: 2. Mount the share
steps.command:
mkdir target-NFS
sudo mount -t nfs 10.129.14.128:/ ./target-NFS/ -o nolock

steps.label: 3. Inspect (names vs raw UIDs) then unmount
steps.command:
ls -l target-NFS/
ls -n target-NFS/
cd ..
sudo umount ./target-NFS

defense.why_it_works: NFS exports can be misconfigured with the 'insecure' option, which 'is dangerous because users can use ports above 1024,' bypassing the OS restriction that only root can bind ports below 1024. The 'no_root_squash' option means 'all files created by root are kept with UID/GID 0,' allowing client-side root to access NFS-mounted files as root. 'root_squash' is the safer default — it assigns root UID/GID 0 to an anonymous UID, preventing remote root access.
defense.prerequisites: Network access to NFS (TCP/UDP 2049 and rpcbind 111).
defense.impact: A list of exports and readable/writable files — especially where an 'insecure'/no_root_squash export misconfiguration exists.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1046 AN1583] Monitor for execution of network enumeration utilities (nmap, netcat, net.exe, ping.exe, tracert.exe) in short succession, particularly when chained with lateral movement tools or system enumeration commands. [AN1584] Sequential ping, arp, or traceroute commands issued from bash scripts or interactive shells to map remote hosts are a strong behavioral indicator.
defense.artifacts: showmount and mount requests in NFS/rpcbind logs; file-access records on exported shares.
defense.prevention:
Avoid the 'insecure' export option. Enable 'root_squash' on all exports. Restrict exports to specific trusted client IPs rather than using wildcards. Prefer NFSv4 which includes Kerberos authentication and ACL support.

[MITRE T1046 M1042] Disable or remove unnecessary services and functionality that expose attack surface. [M1030] Implement network segmentation to limit the set of hosts reachable from any given compromised system. Use firewalls to restrict which source addresses can reach each service port.
defense.misconfiguration: NFS exports are configured with overly permissive options: world-readable (accessible to any host), no_root_squash (remote root user maps to local root), or sync=off. Combined with SSH authorized_keys being writable in an exported directory, this can lead to full system compromise.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# /etc/exports — dangerous NFS export:
/home/user    *(rw,no_root_squash,no_all_squash,sync)
# '*' = any host can mount
# 'rw' = read+write
# 'no_root_squash' = remote root = local root (critical misconfiguration)

# If /home/user/.ssh is on an NFS share:
# Attacker mounts the share, writes their public key to .ssh/authorized_keys
# -> SSH in as that user without a password
defense.secure_config:
# /etc/exports — hardened:
/data/shared    10.10.1.0/24(ro,root_squash,all_squash,sync)
# Specific subnet only, read-only, root_squash (remote root -> nobody)
# all_squash: ALL remote users map to anonymous (anonuid/anongid)

# For read-write shares where needed:
/data/team      10.10.1.100(rw,root_squash,sync,secure)
# 'root_squash' is the minimum — never use no_root_squash
# 'secure' = require source port < 1024 (prevents non-root mounting tricks)

# After editing /etc/exports:
exportfs -ra  # reload exports
exportfs -v   # verify what's published
